title: Credit Model Comparison: Vasicek, CreditRisk+, CreditMetrics, KMV

maps.tested: The sheet's instruction is unusually direct: 'don't get into formulas too much here, but at least know the details of each of the 4 models discussed.'
maps.specifics: A four-way comparison built for the four-statement audit format. Know which is actuarial (CreditRisk+), which is ratings-migration based (CreditMetrics), which underpins the Basel IRB formula (Vasicek), and which is equity-market based (KMV/Merton family).

vardeezReading: CR-10: Very Important; "We can expect different credit risk models comparison to show up on exam. Don't get into formulas too much here, but at least know the details of each of 4 models discussed here. Credit spread risk can be imp too." CR-5: Very Important; "LO 23.d is Imp, LO 23.e & LO 23.f: Imp (LO 23.g for RAROC is imp, but Raroc is more imp in Ops risk)". CR-12: Important; Credit VaR (LO 30.g) is important for the exam, the one-factor model (LO 30.f) is important, LO 30.e is relevant, and the rest are repeats to skim.

los.vardeez: Comparison of credit risk models: know each model, not formulas

selectors.name: CreditRisk+ as actuarial, default-mode model
selectors.what: CreditRisk+ (Credit Suisse Financial Products, 1997) is an actuarial, insurance-style model: the number of defaults is Poisson (mean equal to variance) when PDs are small and independent, and uncertainty in the default rate (gamma, giving a negative binomial) creates default correlation, skews the loss distribution and fattens the tail (Hull: with mean 4, the 99.9th percentile is 11 defaults at sigma = 0 and 98 at sigma = 10). It is a default-mode model: losses are recognised only on default, it does not use the capital structure of the company (that is KMV), and its advantage is the minimum data required.

selectors.name: CreditMetrics as ratings-migration, mark-to-market model
selectors.what: CreditMetrics (JPMorgan, 1997) is built on a rating transition matrix and is a mark-to-market model, not a default-mode one: it books losses from downgrades as well as defaults, and upgrades as gains (negative losses). One-year credit VaR comes from simulating end-of-year ratings with a Gaussian copula (typically equity-return correlation) and revaluing with a credit-spread term structure per rating; default loss is EAD x (1 - R). It is not a rating tool nor a risk pricing model, and it is criticised for homogeneous rating grades and fixed interest rates.

selectors.name: Vasicek as the model under Basel IRB
selectors.what: Vasicek's model is a one-factor Gaussian copula model that gives the worst-case default rate WCDR(T, X) from PD and a single correlation rho; by Gordy's result it underlies the Basel IRB capital formula (T = 1 year, X = 99.9%). It recognises losses from defaults only (downgrades enter the IRB only through the maturity adjustment), takes rho from equity correlations, and incorporates very little tail correlation, which another copula could remedy.

selectors.name: Moody's KMV as equity-market Merton implementation
selectors.what: Moody's KMV is the best-known implementation of Merton's structural model: asset value and volatility are backed out of equity market data, the default point is short-term debt plus half of long-term debt, and the distance to default is mapped to an expected default frequency (EDF) through an empirical distribution of historical default frequencies, not the normal. Default is endogenous, linked to assets and debt, in contrast to reduced-form models where default is an exogenous Poisson jump process.

selectors.name: Four-way comparison: loss recognition, correlation
selectors.what: Compares the four models on what loss is recognised and how default correlation is modelled: Vasicek (defaults only; single Gaussian copula rho from equity correlations), CreditRisk+ (defaults only; correlation arises from uncertainty in the default rate), CreditMetrics (defaults and downgrades, upgrades as gains; Gaussian copula on rating changes using equity correlation), and KMV (default, as EDF at the horizon; correlation not covered in CR-5). On the same assumptions CreditMetrics and CreditRisk+ should give the same long-run loss, with different timing (revaluation losses in each year versus nothing until default).

notSelected: All four learning objectives of the topic (CR-10 d, CR-10 e, CR-5 f, CR-12 g) carry a selector; deliberately left out are the numerical Vasicek WCDR and IRB capital calculations (topic A31), the Merton distance-to-default calculation (A5), the Gaussian copula and default correlation calculations (B3), the credit VaR formula (B1) and credit spread risk (CR-10 f, D5).
